title: A short-lived token proves the workload; grants still decide what it may do
goal: Design secretless AWS workload identity for Databricks and Snowflake without confusing authentication with authorization.
tag: Certification cycle 5 · focused lesson 5 · platform connectivity and access
concept:
A conference badge proves who entered the building. It does not open every room. Workload identity federation works the same way: an AWS role obtains a short-lived signed identity token, a platform policy matches the issuer, audience, and subject, and the platform maps that claim to a non-human identity.

That answers who is calling. SQL grants and platform privileges separately answer what the caller may do. A valid token with no SELECT grant must still be denied.
example: An EKS service account assumes the AWS role orders-etl. The token says issuer = the account-specific AWS issuer, audience = databricks or the configured Snowflake audience, subject = that role. A matching federation rule authenticates the pipeline. The pipeline can read ops.orders because its platform identity has that grant; it cannot drop the catalog.

use_case.when: Use workload identity federation when an unattended AWS workload must call a data platform and you want to remove long-lived platform secrets.
use_case.example: An EKS-hosted Spark control service triggers a Databricks job and a Snowflake validation query using its AWS identity.
use_case.decision: Federate a stable, narrowly scoped workload identity when the runtime can mint verifiable short-lived tokens. Keep a managed secret only when the product, driver, or identity provider does not support federation, and rotate it explicitly.

practice: Change one claim and one grant. Predict whether the request fails at identity matching or at authorization.
boundary: The browser and Python trace model claim matching and one grant only. They do not mint or verify JWT signatures, call AWS STS, Databricks, or Snowflake, reproduce token exchange, role hierarchy, network policy, SCIM, audit logs, driver versions, account boundaries, or cloud-specific failure modes.

questions: The token claims the expected role, but SELECT is not granted. What happens?
Authentication succeeds and the query is denied
The query is automatically allowed
The token adds the grant
Identity proof does not confer object privileges.
Why bind issuer, audience, and subject?
To constrain which signed workload identity can map to the platform identity
To speed up SQL joins
To replace network controls
All three claims narrow the acceptable token context.
When is this model insufficient?
When you need to validate signatures, token exchange, role hierarchy, network policy, and audit evidence
When one table is read
When a token expires quickly
Production identity needs cryptographic, authorization, and operational controls beyond three string comparisons.

title: thenApply wraps the next future; thenCompose follows it
goal: Choose the CompletionStage operator that keeps an asynchronous Java pipeline flat.
concept:
Imagine opening a delivery box and finding another sealed box inside. thenApply transforms a value. If that transform itself returns a future, the result is a future containing another future.

thenCompose is the flat-map form: it waits for the returned stage and completes with that stage's value. Use it when step two is asynchronous and depends on step one.
example: findCustomer() returns CompletionStage<Customer>. loadOrders(customer) also returns a stage. thenApply(this::loadOrders) produces CompletionStage<CompletionStage<Orders>>; thenCompose(this::loadOrders) produces CompletionStage<Orders>. Neither operator supplies a timeout, retry, cancellation policy, or executor capacity.

use_case.when: Use thenCompose when one asynchronous Java operation needs the value from an earlier stage and itself returns a CompletionStage.
use_case.example: Load an account, then call an asynchronous order service for that account.
use_case.decision: Use thenApply for a synchronous mapping such as formatting a name. Use thenCompose for an async dependency. Use thenCombine when independent stages can run in parallel.

practice: Switch between synchronous and asynchronous second steps. Predict the resulting type before revealing the boxes.
boundary: The executable Java example uses already-completed futures, so it proves type/flattening behavior but not scheduling. The browser omits executor choice, latency, exceptional completion, cancellation, timeouts, retries, backpressure, and context propagation.

'+(valid?type:'compose expects a function returning a stage')+'

A nested CompletionStage<CompletionStage<Order>>
A flat CompletionStage<Order>

thenApply maps to whatever value the function returns, including another stage.
Why choose thenCompose?
It flattens the dependent asynchronous stage
It runs independent work in parallel
It adds a retry policy

title: Put things that change together behind one ownership boundary
goal: Use change coupling and business capability—not the org chart alone—to test service and team boundaries.
concept:
A kitchen works faster when the cook who seasons a dish can also taste it. If every change needs a handoff to a separate “spice team,” the organization has drawn a boundary through one unit of work.

A useful service boundary has high cohesion inside and low coupling outside: functions that change together live together, and one team can test, deploy, and operate the capability independently. Team ownership should align to that boundary, not passively dictate it.
example: In six checkout changes, price calculation and promotion eligibility changed together five times. Splitting them into “pricing API” and “campaign API” creates five coordinated releases. Keeping both inside the checkout capability leaves only the less frequent payment-provider contract crossing a boundary.

use_case.when: Use change-coupling evidence when a service split creates coordinated releases, chatty calls, shared schemas, or incidents that bounce between teams.
use_case.example: Checkout, promotion, and payment teams must attend the same release call for nearly every pricing change.
use_case.decision: Co-locate capabilities that change together and can share one operational objective. Keep a boundary when independent scale, security, resilience, or domain language outweighs coordination cost.

practice: Switch between a technical-layer split and a business-capability split. Predict the number of cross-team change pairs.
boundary: This is a six-change coupling sample, not an automatic decomposition algorithm. It omits regulatory segregation, team skill, data ownership, runtime latency, transaction boundaries, scaling, vendor constraints, and future product direction.

title: MCP progress is a live signal—not a durable task record
goal: Use request-scoped progress notifications without mistaking them for resumable work.
concept:
A delivery driver can text “three stops away.” That update reassures you while the trip is active; it is not the warehouse record that lets another driver resume after a crash.

In MCP 2026-07-28, a caller opts in with an opaque _meta.progressToken. The server may send notifications/progress on that request's response stream before the final response. The receiver is not obligated to send them. If work must outlive the stream, use the tasks extension or an explicit durable handle.
example: A corpus-indexing tool emits 20/100 and 70/100 on the same SSE response stream, then returns a final result. If the connection breaks at 70, those notifications do not prove a durable checkpoint exists. A task handle with persisted status is the recovery contract.

use_case.when: Use progress notifications when an in-flight MCP call is slow enough that the client needs liveness and completion estimates.
use_case.example: A harness displays indexing progress while a tool processes 100 documents on one response stream.
use_case.decision: Use request progress for live UX. Use a durable task or explicit handle when the caller must poll, reconnect, resume, or supply later input.

practice: Toggle opt-in and disconnect. Predict which events the client sees and whether it can resume.
boundary: The browser models event order, not an MCP transport. It does not open SSE or STDIO, negotiate a protocol version, handle buffering, validate tokens, persist tasks, estimate trustworthy totals, or implement cancellation and reconnect semantics.

title: A ferroelectric switch can tune frequency-doubled light on a chip

A guitar string can produce a note at twice the original frequency. In optics, second-harmonic generation converts input light at frequency f into light at 2f.

A new Nature Nanotechnology paper integrates 20–40 nm ferroelectric NbOBr₂ with a silicon-nitride microring. title: Matrix jobs finish out of order—give each output a unique name
goal: Prevent nondeterministic GitHub Actions data loss when matrix jobs publish outputs.
concept:
Three runners finish a relay in an unpredictable order. If each writes to the same whiteboard box named digest, the last finisher erases the earlier value.

GitHub does not guarantee matrix job execution order. Matrix job outputs are combined, but duplicate output names overwrite; the last job that runs and sets the name wins. Give every matrix variant a unique output name—or carry many values in artifacts when the payload is not small control data.
example: Linux, macOS, and Windows each produce a test digest. A shared output named digest might end with whichever job finishes last. Names such as digest_linux, digest_macos, and digest_windows produce a stable map regardless of finish order.

use_case.when: Use unique matrix output names when a downstream job must consume one small value from every matrix variant.
use_case.example: A release gate compares one test-manifest digest from Linux, macOS, and Windows.
use_case.decision: Use named outputs for small control values. Use uniquely named artifacts for files or larger evidence, then aggregate them explicitly in a dependent job.

practice: Change finish order and naming strategy. Predict the downstream output map.
boundary: The model covers three successful jobs and output-name collision only. It omits skipped/failed jobs, empty values, output size limits, secret redaction, matrix expansion, artifacts, reruns, needs conditions, and real GitHub scheduling.

title: Content-Digest detects changed bytes—it does not authenticate the sender
goal: Use HTTP digest fields for integrity while keeping sender authentication as a separate control.
concept:
A packing slip can list the exact weight of a sealed box. If the weight differs, you know the contents changed. But anyone who repacks the box can print a new slip.

RFC 9530 defines Content-Digest for HTTP message content bytes and Repr-Digest for representation data. A digest detects mismatch against the supplied value. By itself it does not authenticate, authorize, or provide privacy. Bind the digest into an authenticated HTTP Message Signature when you need to know who sent those bytes.
example: A payment webhook sends {"amount":40} with a SHA-256 Content-Digest. Changing the body to 400 while leaving the header unchanged fails verification. An attacker who changes both body and digest can make the digest match; only a verified signature from a trusted key authenticates the message.

use_case.when: Use Content-Digest when an endpoint needs to detect accidental or malicious content changes across HTTP handling and intermediaries.
use_case.example: A large webhook body is hashed before parsing; the digest field is also covered by the sender's HTTP Message Signature.
use_case.decision: Use a digest for byte integrity. Add a signature for sender authenticity and covered metadata. Use TLS for transport confidentiality; none of these alone is business authorization.

practice: Tamper with the body, recompute the digest, and toggle signature verification. Predict integrity and authenticity separately.
boundary: The browser uses symbolic hashes, not cryptography. It omits Structured Fields encoding, content versus representation transformations, trailers, algorithm agility, canonical signature bases, key distribution, replay protection, clocks, TLS, authorization, and library interoperability.

Authenticated sender

A larger JSON body

walkthrough.limit: The browser uses symbolic hashes, not cryptography. It omits Structured Fields encoding, content versus representation transformations, trailers, algorithm agility, canonical signature bases, key distribution, replay protection, clocks, TLS, authorization, and library interoperability.
